As if we had the facilities, technology, and willing capital at hand just waiting for those politicians' signatures. This is 40 years late. Right now no one actually knows how to mine or process any materials in space. And that's largely because the priority of national space agencies has been the manufacture of state heroes, not an infrastructure for the utilization of space resources and the cultivation of in-space industry. Bottom-line, government isn't in the business of inventing new places for people to go and not pay taxes and we've always understood that astronauts would never be doing the heavy-lifting in space. And so there was never any sincere interest by government in actual space development and Wall Street was always too cowardly to initiate that themselves. So we've got decades of catching-up to do. I think there's very exciting work ahead, but I also think many people have unrealistic expectations about it right now.

For a viable space industrial infrastructure we need to develop launch systems based on an entirely new logistics paradigm that has been ignored for decades; the leveraging of in-space production on reduced launch costs through tolerable yield. The basic idea behind concepts like the Space Systems Loral Aquarius rocket. that is also well suited to emerging non-rocket launch systems like the Quick Launch gas gun The reason launch costs are high is because payload values are high, demanding exceptional degrees of system reliability. That makes sense for human passengers and government hardware, but not for industrial activity. A typical satellite launch has, tied up in its payloads, the equivalent value of an entire automobile manufacturing plant. That's an insane degree of economic risk to try and secure by engineering. By using robotics to make value in space instead of sending it there, you can reduce payloads to low-value commodities and thus reduce the need for extreme engineered launch reliability by the common industry theory of tolerable production yield. But letting a third of unmanned rockets blow-up as we refined them didn't suit the image of technical prowess we wanted to project to Cold War rivals, so we never really explored that. We also need to explore a vast new family of telerobots for orbital and surface applications. We need new compact In-Situ Resource Utilization technology. We need totally different processes of excavation and materials handling in low gravity.

Right now only a handful of people in the world are seriously working on these things and there's no flood of investment capital going towards it. Government sure isn't ponying up that dough, so I wonder about the point of this congressional exercise.
